newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Blinded Egypt volunteer is legend of 1956 Suez war.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Blinded Egypt volunteer is legend of 1956 Suez war.

text.p: In an Egyptian city legendary in the country's long struggle against imperialism, Mohamed Mahran is himself something of a living legend.

Forty years after he lost both his eyes as a volunteer in the Suez war against British troops, he reigns as curator of the Military Museum in Port Said -- a shrine to the very events that brought him fame as a teenager in 1956.

His account of how it happened is both shocking and wholly unsubstantiated. But he tells his tale to anyone who asks, perhaps embellishing it over the years, and the story has become part of the lore of this bastion of Egyptian nationalism.

Port Said, founded in 1859 as excavations for the Suez Canal began, relives its anti-imperialist past every year, burning in public an effigy of General Edmund Allenby, the British high commissioner in Cairo in the turbulent 1920s.
Mahran has pride of place in the city's pantheon of local heroes, a doyen of the veteran irregulars of the Suez war.

"I was the leader of one of the volunteer commando groups entrusted with defending the airport at al-Gameel outside Port Said. I was wounded and taken prisoner by the British soldiers and then sent for treatment to a military hospital in Cyprus. There they removed my eyes," he says.
Mahran says, and most Port Saidis believe, a British doctor gouged them out because he would not tell them Egyptian military plans to repel the French, British and Israeli invasion.
"The military told me to tell or face the worst punishment. I decided to give up my eyes for Egypt," he said.
Forty years later, Mahran bashfully accepts his heroic status and points to a giant portrait of late Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser, who he says is the real star.
"I always wished to die before him," said Mahran. "I saw how the situation was before the 1952 revolution and after that. He was our saviour, our hero."
On July 23, 1952, Nasser and a group of army officers overthrew the monarchy, ending 70 years of British domination.

In July 1956 he announced that Egypt would take over the Suez Canal, a private company owned and run by British and French interests. French and British troops, aided by Israel, invaded in October to reclaim the strategic waterway, which links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea.
They bombed airports in Cairo, but targeted Port Said city and Suez the most. No regular troops went to face them -- the residents took the battle into their own hands.
"The whole residential area was on fire. They bombarded the al-Manakh area, not a single house was left," said Salem Mohamed Saqr, an army major who helped lead the volunteers.

"Then we started fighting in the street. Most of our streets were destroyed and we had a lot of casualties. I'm proud to say it was a good battle, British paratroopers who visited us admitted that, saying "You were heroes and we were not expecting such a defence,'" he added.

"I was a father of five children but I never thought of them or my family. I was thinking of my country where I lived and my descendants will live. I envy now those who were killed, they are martyrs and I would like to be a martyr."

Zakariya Mohamed Ibrahim, who fought with Mahran in Port Said, was 16 at the time. "I also fought in 1967 and 1973 (wars against Israel). And if another war came up, I'll also fight. We're protecting our country, our nation here," he said.
Ibrahim says he was machine-gunned in the back during the Gameel battle and that a "miracle" saved him from paralysis.

"After I was shot, they took me prisoner and flew me to an aircraft carrier. I was dying. I went to a hospital in Limassol (in Cyprus) and was treated. It's a miracle I can still walk," said Ibrahim, a rescue worker in the Suez Canal Authority.
Under pressure from the United States, British prime minister Anthony Eden said all hostilities would end if Egypt and Israel accepted a ceasefire.
Nasser agreed and so did Israeli prime minister David Ben Gurion. In December 1956, British and French troops withdrew.

"It was like a wedding. We were so glad it was over and that our men bravely stood up to the aggression. The cases we used to get at the hospital were so bad I was happy it finished," said Hamidah Ismail, a Red Crescent nurse at the time.
Ismail has one thing to thank the war for.

Listening to the radio in a Port Said hospital in 1957, she heard Mahran recounting his story. Overcome by gratitude and sympathy, she travelled to Cairo to see how she could help treat him, but married him instead.
